notes: Eval 2 (which-skill-to-invoke) is the strongest discriminator: with_skill 3/3, without_skill 1/3. The skill map gives Claude an unambiguous routing table — read-the-error is the explicit entry point for surfaced errors. Without it, Claude defaults to standard debugging instinct (ask for stack trace + speculate) which mixes evidence gathering and hypothesis in one turn.

Eval 3 (anti-pattern-recognition) partially discriminates: with_skill 3/3, without_skill 2/3. The failure is the same in both evals: the baseline redirects to the flow map as a soft prerequisite but doesn't offer the engineer a genuine choice. The hybrid trigger protocol (name + hand back) is a skill-specific behavior the baseline doesn't replicate.

Eval 1 (skipped-gate-mid-session) is the weakest discriminator — both configurations name the risk and redirect to the flow map. The skill response is slightly better (names 'your call' explicitly, cites the anti-pattern), but both fail the conciseness assertion. The conciseness check may be too strict or the skill needs a tighter directive on response length for hybrid trigger.

The with_skill responses are consistently more verbose (+7.5s, +2742 tokens). This is likely because the skill loads into context and the agent generates longer, more structured responses. The verbosity costs performance on the conciseness assertion in eval 1.

Key discriminator: the hybrid trigger protocol — specifically whether Claude names that proceeding is an explicit option and hands the decision back as a real choice. The baseline tends to redirect rather than offer a genuine fork.

Conciseness is a real problem: both with_skill and without_skill fail the 3-sentence threshold in eval 1. The skill should include an explicit length constraint on hybrid trigger responses to enforce this.
